questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a customer's formal request under UK GDPR asking an organization to disclose everything it holds about them, like the one that triggered LTV Global's governance program, is called a ________.
questions.explain: A DSAR (data subject access request) is an individual's formal request to see the personal data an organization holds about them. At LTV Global, answering one took six weeks because no one could say with confidence where all of that person's data actually lived.

questions.prompt: Program Lead Marcus Ibe starts LTV Global's governance program with a plain-language inventory of every system that holds data, before assigning any owners or writing any quality rules. Per this course, why does a landscape review have to come first?
options: You can't assign an owner to a system nobody has named, write a rule against a column nobody has documented, or classify data nobody realizes exists
Regulators require a landscape inventory to be formally filed before any other governance activity can legally begin
A landscape inventory is simply faster to produce than assigning owners, so it's done first purely for efficiency
Data owners refuse to accept assignments until a landscape inventory has been formally approved by the board
questions.explain: A landscape inventory has to come first because every later step depends on knowing what exists: you can't name an owner, write a quality rule, or classify sensitivity for a system or column nobody has documented yet.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the four real criteria this course uses to score a candidate critical data element (CDE).
options: Regulatory impact
Financial impact
Decision impact
Operational impact
Popularity impact — how many people in the company have heard of the element
Alphabetical priority — whether the element's name comes early in the data dictionary
questions.explain: A critical data element earns elevated governance by scoring high on at least one of regulatory impact, financial impact, decision impact, or operational impact. Popularity and alphabetical order are not real criteria — LTV Global's `MarketingOptIn` stayed off the CDE list specifically because it didn't score high on any of the four real criteria.

questions.prompt: Match each LTV Global critical data element to the primary reason it earned elevated governance treatment.
right: High regulatory impact — personal data under UK/California privacy law, and the exact element behind the Lesson 1 DSAR
High financial and decision impact — it rolls up into the number Finance reports to the board
High operational impact — nearly every fulfillment and inventory process keys off it
High regulatory impact — it sits inside PCI scope regardless of how rarely it's queried
questions.explain: Email scored high on regulatory impact because privacy law governs it and it was exactly what the DSAR was about. OrderTotal scored high on financial and decision impact because it feeds the board's revenue number. SKU scored high on operational impact because fulfillment and inventory key off it. CardToken scored high on regulatory impact because PCI scope applies regardless of query frequency.

questions.prompt: At LTV Global, which statement correctly distinguishes a data owner from a data steward?
options: A data owner is accountable for a domain at the business level and can approve a definition or fund a fix; a data steward does the daily work of fixing bad records and answering what a field means.

A data owner is accountable for a domain at the business level and can approve a definition or fund a fix; a data steward is simply a more senior version of the same owner role, with broader authority.
A data steward is accountable for a domain at the business level; a data owner does the daily hands-on work of fixing records.
A data owner and a data steward are the same role under two different job titles, used interchangeably at most companies.
A data owner only exists for domains involving personal data; non-personal domains are managed by stewards alone.
A data steward outranks a data owner whenever a regulatory request like a DSAR is involved.
questions.explain: A data owner (like Renata Silva, VP of Sales) is accountable at the business level — approving definitions, settling disputes, funding fixes. A data steward (like Priya Anand) does the daily hands-on work: fixing bad records, answering what a field means, flagging problems to the owner. They're different jobs held by different people, not two levels of the same role.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B repeats the correct definition of a data owner word for word, which makes it the closest wrong answer — but it redefines the steward as 'a more senior version of the same owner role.' At LTV Global, the owner and steward for Customers.Email are two different named people doing genuinely different jobs, not two ranks of one job.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a usable glossary definition states what the term is, what it explicitly excludes, how it's measured or identified, and ________.
questions.explain: The four-part test requires stating what the term is, what it excludes, how it's measured or identified, and who approved it — the LTV Global glossary entries for Customer, Order Total, and Product all name a specific approving data owner.

questions.prompt: Payments.CardToken is a tokenized reference, not a raw card number, yet LTV Global classifies it as Restricted rather than Confidential. Per this course, why?
options: Classification follows the consequence of exposure, not just the literal content of the field — a breach here still triggers PCI exposure and a mandatory disclosure, regardless of tokenization
Tokenized values are always classified exactly one tier higher than their original data type, as a fixed universal rule
CardToken is actually misclassified; per this course's own scheme, it should be Confidential, not Restricted
Restricted applies only to fields with more than 16 characters, which CardToken happens to have
questions.explain: The tier is driven by the consequence of exposure, not just whether the raw digits are technically present. A breach involving CardToken still triggers PCI exposure and a mandatory incident response, which is exactly why it lands in Restricted even as a token.

questions.code:
-- RULE: ORD-001 — OrderTotal must be positive
SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderTotal
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE OrderTotal <= 0
ORDER BY OrderTotal ASC;
questions.prompt: Why does this LTV Global data quality rule check `OrderTotal <= 0` instead of `OrderTotal < 0`?
options: A zero OrderTotal is just as invalid as a negative one — it almost always means a failed discount calculation or a cancelled order that was never fully voided
SQL Server's WHERE clause requires <= instead of < whenever the column being compared is a DECIMAL type
Using <= instead of < makes the query run noticeably faster on an indexed column
OrderTotal can never actually be negative in practice, so the rule only really needs to catch zero
questions.explain: The rule treats zero as just as invalid as negative, because a zero OrderTotal almost always signals a real problem — a failed discount calculation or a cancelled order that was never fully voided in Atlas — not a legitimate value worth letting through.

questions.prompt: Put these four documented steps of OrderTotal's lineage, from Lesson 8, in the correct order.
items: Atlas — OrderTotal is calculated and written when an order completes
Nightly Atlas-to-Summit load — a scheduled job extracts new and changed orders into a Summit staging table
Summit curated layer — a transformation step cleans and conforms staged rows into fact_Orders, applying the quality rules
Power BI — the Executive Revenue Dashboard queries fact_Orders directly, refreshing each morning
questions.explain: The documented lineage runs: Atlas calculates OrderTotal at order completion, a nightly job lands it in a Summit staging table, the curated layer cleans and conforms it while applying quality rules, and the Executive Revenue Dashboard queries the resulting fact_Orders table each morning.

questions.prompt: Product, Order, and Marketing consent each resolved to one authoritative source in a single meeting, but Customer identity needed a golden-record approach instead. Per this course, why?
options: Atlas, Beacon, and Comet each have a legitimate claim to part of the Customer picture, so no single system reflects the full picture the way one system clearly did for the other three domains
Customer identity is the only domain subject to any regulation at all, which automatically requires a golden record
A golden record was chosen essentially at random, since the three systems' Customer data happened to be identical anyway
Beacon was simply declared the sole authoritative source for Customer identity, the same way it was for marketing consent
questions.explain: Product, Order, and Marketing consent each had one system that clearly did the job no other system did. Customer identity didn't — Atlas, Beacon, and Comet each legitimately held part of the picture, which is exactly why a reconciled golden record, not a single winning system, was needed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about LTV Global's access and retention policy, per this course.
options: No role at LTV Global gets blanket access to Confidential or Restricted data by default — Sales and Support are scoped to records tied to their own accounts or tickets
Payments.CardToken has the shortest retention period of any element in the program
Access policy and retention policy are treated as two entirely unrelated documents with no shared logic
Products.SKU is retained indefinitely, even after discontinuation, because a retired SKU is still needed to make sense of historical orders
Only Finance Analysts are permitted to view Payments.CardToken, since they handle revenue reporting
questions.explain: No role gets blanket Confidential/Restricted access by default, CardToken has the shortest retention window in the program (13 months), and SKU is retained indefinitely for historical order context. Access and retention are treated as one combined policy, not separate documents — and only Risk & Compliance, not Finance Analysts, can view CardToken, with every access logged.

questions.prompt: Which governance KPI from Lesson 11 directly answers the incident that triggered LTV Global's entire governance program, and what's its target?
options: Access request response time — days to fully answer a data subject access request, targeted under 10 business days
CDE ownership coverage — percentage of documented CDEs with a named owner and steward, targeted at 100%
Quality check pass rate — percentage of rows passing the UNION ALL failures report, targeted at 99%+ per rule
Access recertification completion — percentage of Confidential/Restricted role assignments reviewed each quarter, targeted at 100%
questions.explain: Access request response time is a direct answer to the Lesson 1 incident: the DSAR that took six weeks is now a measured, targeted number — under 10 business days — rather than an ad hoc scramble the next time one arrives.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 12, why did LTV Global reject both a fully centralized and a fully decentralized operating model?
options: A fully centralized model would make the small program team a bottleneck for a company with three regions and six business units; a fully decentralized model was exactly what already existed — three systems, three customer records, no one accountable for reconciling them
Both models were rejected purely because neither one is technically compatible with Snowflake or Microsoft Purview
Centralized governance was rejected because it costs strictly more to implement than federated governance in every possible case
Decentralized governance was rejected because it requires a funded self-serve data platform LTV Global didn't have yet
questions.explain: Centralized would bottleneck a small program team across three regions and six business units. Decentralized was simply the status quo that caused the Lesson 1 incident in the first place. The federated hybrid model LTV Global chose instead fit neither extreme.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, why does the demand-forecasting model inherit governance it didn't have to build from scratch, while the support assistant does not?
options: OrderTotal and SKU are already CDEs with owners, stewards, and a quality gate behind them, so the forecasting model's training data is already governed — provided the extract runs after that quality gate
The demand-forecasting model is internal-only, and internal-only models are automatically exempt from every governance check
The support assistant is customer-facing, and customer-facing models never require a model card at all
The forecasting model was built by a VP personally, so his seniority exempts it from the governance checklist
questions.explain: Because OrderTotal and SKU are already CDEs with owners, stewards, and Lesson 7's quality gate behind them, the forecasting model inherits governance that already exists. The support assistant trained on raw, unscrubbed support tickets with no owner and no monitoring plan, so it failed three of the five checks outright.

questions.prompt: Match each zone of LTV Global's target-state architecture to who owns it, per Lesson 14.
right: Whichever domain owner's system feeds it
Jointly owned per the authoritative-source decision, reviewed at the monthly council
questions.explain: Each architecture zone maps onto an existing role from the operating model: domain owners own the raw zone for their source, stewards own the conformed zone for their CDE, the golden zone is jointly owned per the Lesson 9 decision, and the governance office owns the Purview catalog standards themselves.

questions.prompt: Put the five beats of Lesson 17's executive presentation arc in the correct order.
items: The hook — open with the incident that already reached the board
The cost of inaction — state the exposure plainly, in time and dollar terms
What we built — name the outcomes, not the lesson titles
The roadmap — present phases already completed as momentum, with what's next named specifically
The ask — the single, specific, decidable request
questions.explain: The five-beat arc runs: open with the already-known incident, state what inaction costs, name what was actually built as outcomes, present the roadmap as proven momentum, and close with one specific, decidable ask rather than vague support.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: software that scans a resume for keywords before a human reviewer ever sees it is called an ________.
questions.explain: An ATS (applicant tracking system) scans resumes for keywords before a human reviewer sees them — which is why tailoring a resume's wording to match a job posting's actual terms, truthfully, matters for both the ATS and the human reader.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 21, why should a data governance portfolio's Featured section center on documents and diagrams rather than mimicking a data-science portfolio built around a GitHub code repository?
options: Most of what a governance professional actually builds is documents and diagrams — a glossary, a RACI matrix, a lineage diagram, a strategy deck — alongside a smaller amount of actual SQL, so the portfolio should honestly reflect that mix
Code repositories are not permitted on LinkedIn profiles under its terms of service
Governance roles never involve any SQL at all, so including code would misrepresent the role entirely
A documents-and-diagrams portfolio is always more impressive to reviewers than a code repository, regardless of role
questions.explain: A governance portfolio should honestly reflect what the work actually is: mostly documents and diagrams, with a smaller amount of real SQL — forcing it into a code-repository-centric shape would misrepresent the role, not make it more impressive.

questions.prompt: Match each governance portfolio artifact to the follow-up question it needs to survive, per Lesson 22.
right: "Why does this definition say 90 days and not 60?"
"Walk me through this WHERE clause — which rows does it catch, and why are those the bad ones?"
"Who is the single Accountable role here, and why that person and not someone else?"
"What would you do if the finance number diverged at an earlier hop than the one shown here?"
questions.explain: A glossary entry needs to survive a question about a specific stated detail like a time period. SQL checks need to survive a line-by-line walkthrough of the WHERE clause. A lineage diagram needs to survive a question about tracing a different break point. A RACI matrix needs to survive a challenge on exactly who holds the single Accountable role.

questions.prompt: Put the four parts of Lesson 23's structure for explaining a capstone project in an interview in the correct order.
items: Situation — the problem, stated in one sentence
Task — what the engagement needed to deliver
Result — what the finished program demonstrates, framed as a capability, not an invented metric
questions.explain: The structure runs Situation, Task, Action, Result — stating the problem, what needed to be delivered, what was actually built, and finally what the work demonstrates as a capability, rather than a fabricated statistic the project never actually measured.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how a data governance hiring process's round mix shifts depending on role flavor, per this course?
options: A Data Steward-flavored role leans heavily on scenario and domain questions, while a Governance Manager-flavored role leans on stakeholder management and operating-model design conversations.
A Data Steward-flavored role leans heavily on scenario and domain questions, while a Governance Manager-flavored role leans almost entirely on a timed SQL coding screen instead.
Every governance role, regardless of flavor, runs through the exact same fixed sequence of interview rounds in the exact same order, with no round ever added, skipped, or reweighted for any title.
A Privacy/Compliance-flavored role never includes any technical SQL or data-profiling questions at all.
The recruiter screen is where SQL and data-profiling skills are evaluated most rigorously.
Role flavor only ever affects the offer stage, never any of the earlier interview rounds.
questions.explain: A steward-flavored role leans on scenario and domain questions; a governance-manager-flavored role leans on stakeholder management, KPI reporting, and operating-model design instead. Role flavor shifts the whole mix of rounds, not just the offer stage, and the recruiter screen is explicitly non-technical.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct first half about the Data Steward flavor, which is what makes it tempting — but it swaps the real description of a Governance Manager-flavored role (stakeholder management, KPI reporting, operating-model design) for 'almost entirely a timed SQL coding screen,' which this course actually attributes to the Governance Analyst flavor's technical screen, not the manager flavor.

questions.prompt: Marketing says a company has 50,000 customers; Finance says 38,000, and both numbers are technically correct by their own definition. Per Lesson 25's recommended approach, what should you do first?
options: Get both definitions in writing, then find (or establish) the named owner for the Customer domain, and bring both definitions to that owner for a single authoritative decision
Average the two numbers and report 44,000 as a reasonable compromise figure
Tell Marketing their number is wrong, since Finance's systems are generally considered more authoritative
Ignore the discrepancy, since both departments are technically correct by their own internal definitions
questions.explain: The strong answer treats this as a missing or competing glossary term, not a data bug: get both definitions in writing, find the domain's named owner (or flag the missing ownership as the real problem), and get one authoritative decision — possibly two clearly separate, named terms if both concepts are legitimately different.

questions.code:
SELECT o.OrderId, o.CustomerId
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN dbo.Customers AS c
    ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
WHERE c.CustomerId IS NULL
  AND o.CustomerId IS NOT NULL;
questions.prompt: Why does this orphan-detection query need `AND o.CustomerId IS NOT NULL` in addition to `c.CustomerId IS NULL`?
options: Without it, a legitimately-NULL foreign key (such as a guest checkout with no customer at all) would be miscounted as an orphaned row, when it's actually a completeness question, not a referential integrity failure
Without it, the LEFT JOIN would raise a syntax error, since SQL Server requires at least two conditions in every WHERE clause on a joined query
Without it, the query would simply return every row in dbo.Orders, regardless of whether CustomerId matched anything
Without it, the query would run correctly but take significantly longer to execute against a large table
questions.explain: A NULL foreign key usually means 'no customer, intentionally' — a guest checkout — which is a completeness question, not an orphaned row. Without the extra condition, every legitimately-NULL order would get miscounted as an orphan.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about metadata and lineage, per Lesson 27.
options: A business glossary captures what a concept means to the business; a data dictionary captures technical structure like data type and nullability
A data dictionary is typically owned by a business steward, the same way a glossary term is
Column-level lineage costs more to build and maintain than table-level lineage
Column-level lineage is always the better choice, regardless of the situation
Impact analysis walks downstream from a proposed change to see what depends on it; root-cause analysis walks upstream from a symptom to find where it originated
questions.explain: The glossary covers business meaning while the dictionary covers technical structure. Column-level lineage costs more than table-level, because it requires parsing the actual transformation logic. Impact analysis looks downstream before a change; root-cause analysis looks upstream after a symptom appears. A data dictionary is owned by whichever system contains the data, not a business steward, and column-level lineage isn't always the better choice — it's reserved for high-value or high-risk pipelines.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 28, what's the correct distinction between data governance and data security, as a governance analyst should explain it in an interview?
options: Governance defines who should have access and why; security teams implement and enforce how that access is technically controlled
Governance and data security are two names for the exact same function, just used by different departments
Security defines who should have access; governance only audits security's decisions after the fact
Governance exists only to approve security's technical implementations, with no independent policy role of its own
questions.explain: Governance defines who should have access and why — the policy layer. Security teams implement and enforce how that access is technically controlled. Governance isn't a rubber stamp on security's work, and it isn't the same function under a different name.

questions.prompt: A governance analyst needs to update an executive sponsor, a business stakeholder who owns the affected data, and an engineer who'll implement a control, all about the same underlying fact. Per Lesson 29, what should change between the three versions?
options: Which part of the message leads and how much detail comes first — the underlying facts stay the same across all three
The underlying facts themselves, since each audience should be told a different version of what actually happened
Nothing at all — the exact same message, in the exact same order and detail, should be sent to all three audiences
Only the executive sponsor actually needs to be told; the other two can find out through their own channels
questions.explain: Audience layering changes which part of the message leads and how much detail comes first — executives want business impact and the ask, stakeholders want what it means for their team, engineers want the precise technical detail — without ever changing the underlying facts themselves.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: DAMA International's broad data management certification, aligned to the DMBOK framework, is called the ________.
questions.explain: CDMP (Certified Data Management Professional) is DAMA International's credential, aligned to the DMBOK and the DAMA Wheel this path's foundations course already taught — the certification most directly matched to this catalog's own governance vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 31, why does giving a data engineer the 'why' behind a policy — not just the 'what' — matter when asking them to implement a control such as row-level masking?
options: An engineer who understands the reason behind a rule makes better implementation calls when edge cases come up that the policy didn't explicitly anticipate
Engineers are contractually required to be told the reason before they're allowed to implement any control
Explaining the why is purely a courtesy with no actual effect on how the control ends up being implemented
Without a stated reason, SQL Server will refuse to apply a masking policy at all
questions.explain: Explaining the why matters because it changes real outcomes: an engineer who understands that a field needs masking because it's classified restricted PII will make better calls when an edge case the policy didn't explicitly anticipate comes up.

questions.prompt: Why does this course recommend redirecting a 'what are your salary expectations' question toward the employer's budgeted range, or answering with a researched range rather than a single number, per Lesson 32?
options: Whoever names a number first anchors the rest of the negotiation, so naming your own single invented figure first gives up leverage you don't need to give up
Naming any salary number at all, in any form, is illegal in salary negotiations in every jurisdiction
A range is legally required in every jurisdiction this course covers, while a single number is not
It's simply a politeness convention with no real strategic effect on the outcome of the negotiation
questions.explain: Whoever names a number first anchors the rest of the conversation. Redirecting to the budgeted range, or answering with a researched range instead of a single invented figure, avoids giving up that anchoring leverage for no reason.

questions.prompt: Match each rung of the governance career ladder to its typical focus, per Lesson 34.
right: Executing defined governance tasks — glossary entries, data quality checks, documentation, classification of individual datasets
Owning a full domain or process, mentoring newer analysts, handling ambiguous requests without constant guidance
Running the governance program itself — stakeholder management, roadmaps, KPIs, budget and resourcing conversations
Designing how governance works at an enterprise and technical-architecture level — metadata architecture, catalog and lineage architecture, policy-as-code
questions.explain: The ladder runs from executing defined tasks at the entry level, to owning a full domain with judgment at senior analyst, to running the program itself at the manager rung, to designing enterprise-level governance systems at the architect rung — a shift in the kind of problem you're trusted to own at each step, not just a title change.
